true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Duplicate and blacklist checks are case-sensitive

uniqueGuests compares guest === attendee.email and blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing only the env list. Zod's email() does not normalize case, so Guest@x.com is inserted again when guest@x.com is already an attendee, and a blacklisted address is accepted if the casing differs. That creates duplicate attendee rows and bypasses BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admin/owner check uses AND, so neither role alone can add guests

isTeamAdminOrOwner is computed as isTeamAdmin(...) && isTeamOwner(...). A user who is only a team admin, or only a team owner, fails both this flag and the organizer/attendee checks and gets FORBIDDEN. The name and the usual Cal.com permission model require OR. teamId ?? 0 also runs those checks against team 0 for personal event types, which cannot succeed. Team admins/owners therefore cannot add guests to team bookings unless they are also the booking user or an attendee.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Emails are keyed off the raw guest list, not the guests actually inserted

sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests) receives the original input, not uniqueGuests. The mailer treats any address in that list as a brand-new invitee and sends AttendeeScheduledEmail (full confirmation, ICS REQUEST, meeting link) instead of AttendeeAddGuestsEmail. Re-submitting an existing attendee's address therefore sends them another booking confirmation, and blacklisted addresses that were filtered out of the DB write can still be treated as new guests if they were already on the booking.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Add-guest emails ignore event-type email disable flags

sendAddGuestsEmails always emails the organizer, every team member, and every attendee. Unlike sendScheduledEmails and sendLocationChangeEmails, it never consults disableStandardEmails for host or attendee. Event types that turned standard emails off still blast guest-added mail and full scheduled emails (with ICS and video links) to every new address.

false_negatives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Calendar attendee update uses the actor's credentials, not the organizer's

getUsersCredentials(ctx.user) and EventManager are built from the logged-in caller, while booking.user.credentials (already loaded) is ignored. updateCalendarAttendees then runs as whoever clicked Add. When a team admin or attendee adds guests, the organizer's Google/Outlook event is not updated (or the call fails), so new guests never appear on the host calendar even though they were written to the booking.

Custom email title and subject are overridden by spread props

Both AttendeeAddGuestsEmail and OrganizerAddGuestsEmail set title, subject, and headerType, then spread {...props} afterward. Component props that include those fields replace the guest-specific copy, so the React email renders as a normal scheduled email (and OrganizerAddGuestsEmail's callToAction={null} is likewise overwritten). The nodemailer subject can still be correct, but the HTML body title/CTA will not match the 'guests added' intent whenever those props are passed through renderEmail.

No booking status, time, or seat-capacity checks before adding guests

The handler updates any booking by id once the caller passes the permission check. Cancelled, rejected, and past bookings still get new attendee rows and confirmation emails with the meeting link. Seated event types (seatsPerTimeSlot) are not checked, so createMany can push attendance past the seat limit and treat extra people as full attendees rather than seats. There is also no guard that the event type allows additional guests.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount update is a lost-update read-modify-write

Both failure paths set retryCount to the value read at the start of the loop (`reminder.retryCount + 1`) instead of an atomic increment. Overlapping cron invocations can both read the same count and write the same next value, so failures are under-counted and the retryCount > 1 delete never trips. The reminder then keeps being rescheduled indefinitely, which is the bug this change is supposed to fix. Use Prisma's `{ increment: 1 }` so concurrent runs cannot collapse retries.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry cleanup deletes every workflow reminder, not just SMS

The new deleteMany OR branch matches any WorkflowReminder with retryCount > 1 and does not constrain method, scheduled, or scheduledDate. WorkflowReminder is shared by EMAIL, SMS, and WHATSAPP. This SMS cron therefore deletes other channels' rows (and already-scheduled SMS rows) as soon as retryCount exceeds 1, even if those reminders are still valid and were never handled by this job. That silently drops reminders the cron should not own.

false_positives.candidate:
Missing phone or empty message never increments retryCount

retryCount is only incremented inside `if (message?.length > 0 && sendTo)` or in the catch around that block. If sendTo is missing/empty (the invalid-or-absent phone case this PR is meant to stop) or the rendered message is empty, the reminder is neither scheduled nor counted as a failure, and the earlier `continue` when workflowStep or booking is missing has the same gap. Those rows stay scheduled=false with retryCount 0 and are selected again on every cron run until scheduledDate is in the past, so the infinite reschedule loop remains for the failure mode described in the PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
findMany removed, so authorization is no longer applied at the query boundary

The public `findMany` method, which always merged authorization and filter conditions into `bookingTimeStatusDenormalized.findMany`, was replaced by `getBaseConditions()` returning a SQL fragment. No other file in this PR updates callers. Any existing caller of `findMany` will fail to compile, and authorization is now optional: a caller that queries `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` without interpolating this fragment reads rows with no scope check. The old method also merged caller `where` (dates, status, select). `getBaseConditions` cannot express that, and because a `Prisma.Sql` object is always truthy the trailing branches that return only filters or `1=0` are dead—the fragment is easy to misuse and nothing in the service still enforces it.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
ANY() bound to a JS array will not produce a valid Postgres array predicate

Team and org authorization now emit `"teamId" = ANY(${teamIds})` and `"userId" = ANY(${userIds})` (also at the team-scope builder around line 201). Prisma.sql does not turn a JavaScript number[] into a PostgreSQL array parameter; the array is either expanded into multiple placeholders (`ANY($1, $2, ...)`, a syntax error) or bound as text/json, which fails at runtime with an operator/type error such as `integer = text` or `op ANY/ALL (array) requires array on right side`. Those are the only predicates that restrict team and org insights, so team/org queries throw or cannot be applied. Use `IN (${Prisma.join(ids)})` (already guarded against empty lists) or an explicitly cast single array parameter, and run the resulting SQL against Postgres.

Team and org SQL is never executed, so broken ANY() predicates still pass

Authorization tests only deep-equal `Prisma.Sql` objects against another `Prisma.sql` template that uses the same `ANY(${array})` construction. That comparison checks string/value shape, not that Postgres accepts the query. The only `$queryRaw` (around line 481) is user scope (`userId = $1 AND teamId IS NULL`) and never hits `= ANY(...)`. A syntax or type error in the team/org authorization SQL therefore ships with a green suite. Execute those fragments against `BookingTimeStatusDenormalized` for owner, admin, member, empty team, and a team that is not a child of the org.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Empty updateMany will throw after cache write

fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache calls SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {}) to bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt. Prisma rejects updateMany when data is empty, so this throws after the free/busy cache has already been written. Webhook and cache-refresh paths that reach this method will fail, and the timestamp the comment says it is updating never changes.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' is macOS-only

The script rewrites GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL with sed -i '' (BSD sed). GNU sed on Linux treats the empty string as the script and errors, so the helper cannot update .env on Linux even when Tunnelmole starts successfully.

Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

false_positives.candidate:
Cache delete does not refresh calendar query

deleteCacheMutation only toasts and calls the optional onSuccess prop. Unlike the disconnect mutation in the same component, it never invalidates viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars. After a successful delete the dropdown still shows the previous cache_last_updated until something else refetches, so the action looks like it failed.

Delete cache leaves Google watches running

deleteCacheHandler only deletes CalendarCache rows after confirming the credential belongs to the caller. It does not stop the Google channel subscriptions stored on SelectedCalendar (googleChannelId / resourceId). Active watches will call fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache and immediately rewrite the cache, so "Delete cached data" does not stick and the UI can show a fresh timestamp again on the next refresh.

dev:cron now depends on undeclared tsx

dev:cron was changed from ts-node to npx tsx cron-tester.ts, but tsx is not a dependency of @calcom/web (ts-node still is). Under Yarn 3, npx will try to fetch tsx outside the lockfile and fail offline or in CI, so the cron tester script no longer runs reliably.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder cancellation is never awaited

The new cancel path calls deleteScheduledEmailReminder / deleteScheduledSMSReminder inside forEach and never awaits those promises (they are also no longer included in the Promise.all that used to wait for reminder DB writes). deleteScheduledEmailReminder only persists cancelled=true (or deletes the row) inside that promise. On a Next.js/serverless handler the process can freeze as soon as the response is returned, so the flag is often never written and the cron never sees the reminder. The same un-awaited forEach is used in packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx (requestReschedule, around line 488) and packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx (disabled event types / edited steps). Cancelled and rescheduled bookings will keep sending workflow emails.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete reintroduces the 100-cancel cap and skips retry

When immediateDelete is true (reschedule in handleNewBooking.ts, workflow delete, and deleted workflow steps), the function POSTs status=cancel to SendGrid and returns without setting cancelled or deleting the WorkflowReminder row. That is the same immediate scheduled_sends cancel the PR says fails once 100 cancellations are pending. The error is only console.logged, cancelled stays null, so the cron will not retry, and the email is still sent. Reschedule — one of the two cases this PR claims to fix — always takes this path. immediateDelete also does not remove the DB row, so a failed cancel cannot be recovered later.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
One SendGrid error aborts every pending cancel

Cancellation is a single try around the whole for-loop, and prisma.workflowReminder.delete promises are only executed in Promise.all after every SendGrid call succeeds. If any request throws (null referenceId, already-cancelled batch, rate limit, one bad batch_id), the catch logs and exits: remaining reminders are not cancelled, and deletes for batches that were already cancelled in SendGrid never run. On the next cron those already-cancelled batches are retried first, fail again, and block every later reminder indefinitely. Each reminder needs its own try/catch, and the DB row should be deleted only after that reminder's cancel succeeds. The query also does not restrict method to EMAIL or require a non-null referenceId, so an SMS sid or null batch_id can poison the loop.

Paid cancellation returns before reminders are cancelled

When bookingToDelete.paid is set, the handler refunds, marks the booking REJECTED, awaits apiDeletes, and returns at the 'Booking successfully cancelled' path. The workflow-reminder cancellation added below that return (the forEach over updatedBookings.workflowReminders) never runs for paid bookings. Those bookings still have scheduled SendGrid/Twilio reminders, so cancelling a paid booking continues to send workflow emails.

Past cancelled reminders are deleted before SendGrid cancel

The cron first deleteMany's every EMAIL WorkflowReminder whose scheduledDate is already <= now, including rows with cancelled=true, and only afterwards looks up cancelled reminders to POST a SendGrid batch cancel. Any cancelled reminder whose send time has passed (cron delayed, or the 15-minute job running after a reminder that was inside the one-hour window) is removed from the database without ever calling /v3/user/scheduled_sends. SendGrid still has the batch and delivers the email, and there is no row left to retry. Cancellation must run before that delete, and past cancelled rows must not be removed until the batch cancel succeeds.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
async forEach drops calendar and video deletion

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...) does not wait for the callback. getCalendar is now async, so the first await yields before deleteEvent or deleteMeeting is even called, and the returned promises are discarded. The surrounding try/catch cannot see rejections. Reschedule then sends the email and returns while cleanup is still pending, so on a short-lived server the old calendar event and video meeting are often never deleted and failures are unhandled. Await Promise.all over the refs (or use for...of) and await both getCalendar and deleteMeeting.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports still load every app at module init

Every app is started with a top-level import() inside the appStore object literal, so evaluating this module immediately begins loading all app packages. Callers cannot load only the app they need, which defeats the stated async-import goal: startup still pays for every integration, and a failed chunk becomes a rejected promise on that key the first time it is awaited. Wrap each entry in a function (e.g. applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")) and invoke it only at the lookup site.

Recurring cancel never joins calendar deletes

When cancelling all remaining recurring instances, credentials are walked with forEach(async). getCalendar and deleteEvent are awaited only inside that callback, and apiDeletes.push runs after those awaits. The later await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes)) therefore runs before any of those pushes, so recurring calendar events are not deleted and errors never fail the handler. The non-recurring branch correctly uses a for...of and pushes the promise before awaiting the batch; this branch should do the same (or return promises into apiDeletes without an inner await).

async forEach drops calendar and video deletion

Same pattern as vital reschedule: forEach(async) is not joined. Because getCalendar must be awaited, calendar.deleteEvent and deleteMeeting are no longer even started before Reschedule returns and the try/catch cannot catch their errors. Previous-slot calendar events and video meetings are left behind on reschedule. Replace forEach with an awaited Promise.all or for...of.

requestReschedule does not wait for integration cleanup

bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async ...) fires getCalendar/deleteEvent and deleteMeeting without awaiting the callbacks. The mutation then sends the reschedule email and completes. Those promises are not part of the procedure's returned work, so calendar deletes and video deletes are raced against process exit and their rejections are unhandled. The booking is already marked CANCELLED, so a dropped delete leaves a ghost event on the user's calendar. Await Promise.all of the per-reference work before sendRequestRescheduleEmail.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours fallback allows non-working days

When no date override applies, availability is rejected only if workingHours.find returns a row whose days include the slot's UTC weekday and whose range does not contain the slot. If the fixed host simply does not work that weekday, no row matches, find returns undefined, and the function falls through to the busy check and returns available. Round-robin slots generated from other hosts are therefore still bookable on days the fixed host has no working hours. The end bound is also wrong: both start and end are computed from slotStartTime, so a slot that starts inside hours but runs past endTime is not rejected, and those minute values are UTC while WorkingHours may be organizer-local minutes.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
All-day block override never matches

A blocked day is detected with `dayjs(date.start).add(...) === dayjs(date.end).add(...)`. Dayjs instances are compared by object identity, so this is always false even when the instants are equal. The callback then fails to reject the slot, dateOverrideExist is set, and the following branch returns true. An override whose start equals its end (the usual "unavailable all day" marker) makes the fixed host look fully available that day instead of blocked.

false_positives.candidate:
Date override match skips busy-time check

In checkIfIsAvailable, once any date override is found for the slot's calendar day and the slot is treated as inside that override, the function returns true immediately. It never runs the busy-interval check below. Fixed hosts (and round-robin hosts) with a date override can therefore be offered slots that overlap existing bookings or calendar busy times, so the booking page will show times that cannot actually be booked.

Multiple overrides are treated as an intersection

dateOverrides.find returns the first override for which the callback returns true, and the callback returns true when the slot is merely outside that one window (before its start or after its end). If a host has two override ranges on the same day, a slot inside the second range is still outside the first, so find succeeds and checkIfIsAvailable returns false. Only a slot that sits inside every override at once survives. Split date overrides (for example morning and afternoon) disappear from round-robin availability.

Override timezone shift wraps and can throw

The new override window is built with dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone). timeZone is optional on TimeRange; if a caller omits it, tz(undefined) throws and slot generation fails. Date.toString() is a locale string, so the parsed instant (and thus the DST offset) is unreliable. The shifted time is then reduced with .hour() and .minute() only, so an offset that crosses midnight wraps to the same invitee day (23:00 plus two hours becomes 01:00, or a negative offset becomes a late evening). buildSlots also drops ranges where start >= end, so a wrapped override window produces no slots or slots on the wrong day.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Sender comparison assumes metadata shape and crashes instead of failing closed

The mismatch check indexes integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] with no existence or type guard. build_integration only stores sender when state already has it, so existing rows and installs created before the webhook (or without a sender payload) have no sender key. false_negatives.golden_comment: OAuth state uses pipeline.signature (static) instead of a per-request random value

false_positives.candidate:
Installer identity check is skipped when no Integration row exists

GitHubInstallation only compares pipeline state github_authenticated_user to metadata sender when an Integration for installation_id already exists, has no OrganizationIntegration, and is ACTIVE. If Integration.DoesNotExist, dispatch returns pipeline.next_step() immediately and never consults the OAuth login. Installation IDs are predictable integers and are supplied by the client (query string or earlier bind_state). An attacker who starts the install pipeline in their own Sentry org and supplies a victim installation_id before the installation webhook creates the Integration will pass this gate, and build_integration will attach that GitHub App installation to the attacker org with no check that the OAuth user is the installer. That is the mismatch this change claims to reject, and it is unenforced on the normal first-install path.

OAuth authorize URL is built by string concatenation without encoding

The authorize redirect interpolates client_id, state, and redirect_uri into the query string with no urlencode. redirect_uri comes from absolute_uri() and is not escaped, so any reserved character (&, #, ?) splits or drops parameters. state and client_id are likewise unescaped. A crafted or future redirect_uri can change which parameters GitHub sees (for example dropping or replacing state), which weakens the CSRF check this view just added. Use urllib.parse.urlencode for the query.

Token exchange omits redirect_uri required by the authorize request

OAuthLoginView sends redirect_uri on the GitHub authorize redirect, but the subsequent POST to the access-token URL only sends code, client_id, and client_secret. GitHub requires the same redirect_uri on the token exchange when it was included in the authorization request. The exchange will be rejected, access_token will be missing, and every install will fall through to the generic invalid-installation error. Tests stub the token endpoint and never assert the POST body, so they do not catch this.

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:

AssignmentSource.queued uses timezone.now() as a dataclass default, which is evaluated once when the class body runs, not when an instance is created. Every AssignmentSource therefore shares the same queued value from process import, so the field cannot record when an inbound assignment was actually queued. It needs field(default_factory=timezone.now) (or an explicit argument). As written, any later ordering, dedupe, or staleness check on queued is wrong.

That aborts sync_group_assignee_inbound after the Sentry assignee write and drops outbound sync to every other linked integration, not only the originating one. to_dict/from_dict need a JSON-safe queued value (for example an ISO string parsed back to datetime); from_dict currently does cls(**input_dict) and also returns None on TypeError, which would fail open and re-enable the sync loop if the payload cannot be rebuilt.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.

test_basic monkeypatches time.sleep to a no-op, then calls time.sleep(0.1) after setting current_drift, with a comment that this gives the flusher time to observe the new clock. That call is the patched sleep, so it returns immediately. join() sets stopped=True before it waits, so the flusher thread must have already flushed or the test fails. The added sleep does not close that race; the test only passes if the thread is scheduled in the gap between the drift write and join().

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.

true_positives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
join() can exit without stopping flusher processes

join() spends the entire timeout on next_step.join() first, then breaks out of the process loop as soon as the deadline has passed, before process.terminate(). The previous single-process join always terminated the flusher after the wait. With a timeout (Arroyo's join_timeout, including rebalance), every flusher process can therefore be left running. Those processes are only daemonized, not reaped, and close() intentionally does not stop them, so after partition revocation they keep calling flush_segments/produce on shards that another consumer now owns. That duplicates buffered segments to Kafka and leaves zombie processes across rebalances because nothing ever process.join()s them.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.

Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.

false_positives.candidate:
Restart overlaps flushers and leaks the old process

_ensure_processes_alive kills a hung or dead flusher and immediately calls _create_process_for_shards, which overwrites self.processes[process_index] and self.buffers[process_index] without join()ing or waiting for the old process to exit. kill() is asynchronous, and threads (the produce_to_pipe path) are not stopped at all because terminate is gated on isinstance(..., multiprocessing.Process). Until the old worker actually dies it keeps flushing the same shards as the new one, so both can produce the same segments and race on done_flush_segments. The dropped Process handle is never reaped, so each restart also leaks a zombie and that worker's Redis/Kafka clients.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Graceful shutdown commits before workers drain

close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before queue_pool.shutdown() drains and processes remaining items. The commit loop exits after at most one commit of work that already finished. Items still queued are then processed in OrderedQueueWorker during shutdown, complete_offset runs, and nothing commits those offsets. On restart Kafka redelivers them, so uptime results are applied twice (duplicate incidents/check-ins) on every deploy or consumer restart. join() also ignores its timeout and always calls close(), so Arroyo cannot bound shutdown time.

Offsets are committed from a background thread

A daemon commit_thread calls the Arroyo commit callback every second. Arroyo invokes submit/poll/close on the stream processor thread and expects commit() on that same thread; the callback updates consumer offset state and issues librdkafka commits. Calling it concurrently with poll/submit can race the consumer's in-flight commit, raise, or commit a mix of offsets the processor thread is not currently assigned. Commit should be driven from poll() (or another call on the processing thread), not a side thread.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure

Each worker queue is queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and submit() always returns after put(). The class docstring claims natural backpressure when queues fill, but the consumer thread never blocks. If result handling is slower than intake, queued WorkItems (including full Kafka messages) grow without limit until the process OOMs. Because commits cannot advance past the oldest outstanding offset, consumer lag also grows and the member can exceed max.poll.interval and be kicked from the group.

Strategy close kills the shared pool and later messages are acked unprocessed

FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategies, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (and terminate()) always call queue_pool.shutdown(). Arroyo closes the strategy on partition revoke/rebalance and then calls create_with_partitions again on the same factory. After shutdown, Queue.put raises queue.ShutDown. submit() catches that, and the except path add_offset+complete_offset without ever running the result processor. The new strategy's commit thread then treats those offsets as done and commits them. Every message after the first rebalance is acknowledged and dropped. The offset tracker is also not reset, so a new assignment can still commit offsets for revoked partitions.

Worker failures still advance the commit point

OrderedQueueWorker catches every Exception from result_processor, logs it, and always complete_offset in finally. get_committable_offsets then treats the message as processed and the commit loop commits past it. The strategy docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing. A transient DB or downstream error is therefore acknowledged and never retried, so uptime results are silently dropped. The same swallow exists in submit() when decode or grouping raises, which also marks the offset complete.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial cache key aliases different resources

userPermDenialCacheKey joins name and parent with '_' and both values are UIDs that may themselves contain underscores. Distinct pairs such as name "a_b" / parent "c" and name "a" / parent "b_c" produce the same key. A cached deny for one pair is then treated as a deny for the other, so Check can reject a resource the user is allowed to access for up to 30 seconds.

The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.

Denial cache ignores newly granted permissions

Check returns Allowed=false as soon as a denial-cache entry exists for (namespace, subject, action, name, parent), before consulting either the permission cache or the database. Entries are written for every deny and kept for shortCacheTTL (30s), and nothing deletes them when a role, team, or creator grant later adds that scope. A user who was denied on a dashboard or folder they then create or are granted will keep getting denied until TTL, which is the failure this PR is meant to fix. The same sticky deny is recorded when checkPermission fails only because the folder tree cache is stale, so a parent-folder grant on a just-created child stays denied even after the tree would have allowed it.

List returns immediately when getCachedIdentityPermissions hits, and never re-reads the DB if the cached scope map is missing a dashboard or folder created after the entry was stored. Only the in-proc client is switched to NoopCache. newRemoteRBACClient still wraps the gRPC client in a local cache with a 30s expiry. Cloud/remote callers therefore keep returning the previous allow/deny for a newly created dashboard or folder until that client entry expires, so the server-side requery never runs and the reported creator access bug remains in that mode.

$__range queries are interpolated before the no-split guard

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. true_positives.matched_candidate:

Every caller that observed a nil cache therefore reloads and then unconditionally assigns entryPointAssetsCache = result. If one of those loads succeeds and a later one fails, result is nil and the assignment clears the good cache. Later non-dev callers then miss the cache and fail (or stampede the manifest read again) even though a valid EntryPointAssets was already published. Only store the pointer when err == nil and the cache is still empty (or always keep the previous value on error), and repeat the nil check after Lock.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
BuildIndex no longer serializes same-key builds

BuildIndex used to hold cacheMu for the entire build. The lock now covers only the cache insert, and nothing single-flights a key. getOrCreateIndex is check-then-act (GetIndex, then BuildIndex if missing), and handleEvent plus Search can do that concurrently for a namespace that was not built at startup. Two BuildIndex calls for the same key both run bleve.New (file indexes collide on the same directory and the second New fails; memory indexes both succeed), both can pass the builder, and the later cache write overwrites the earlier *bleveIndex without closing it. Callers can also observe a nil index and start yet another build while the first is still running. TotalDocs ranges b.cache with no lock, so a concurrent cache write can panic the map. The old global lock was slow but prevented this; a per-key lock or singleflight is required, and every cache read must take cacheMu.

Bleve BuildIndex span is not the parent of index work

The PR's trace fix reassigns ctx from tracer.Start in searchSupport.init, searchSupport.build, and GetResourceStats, but BuildIndex still does `_, span := b.tracer.Start(ctx, ...)`. The span is ended, yet the context passed into the builder and ListIterator is the parent context, so the bleve BuildIndex span is a sibling of the DB and document-build spans rather than their parent. Any further bleve work in this function also will not carry the span. Use `ctx, span := b.tracer.Start(...)` and pass that ctx downward, matching the other call sites in this change.

Failed constructor leaves background work running

NewResourceServer creates a cancelable context, stores cancel on the server, then calls Init. On error it logs and returns nil without calling cancel or Stop. Init can already have started searchSupport's WatchWriteEvents poller (that one uses context.Background(), so cancel would not stop it anyway) and, if initWatcher ran, a broadcaster tied to s.ctx. The caller only receives an error and has no server handle to shut those goroutines down, so a failed startup leaks pollers and DB work for the process lifetime. Cancel and stop any watchers before returning the error, and tie the search watch to s.ctx instead of context.Background().

Index init workers race on shared err

init launches one errgroup goroutine per namespace, and each does `_, _, err = s.build(...)` on the single err variable from GetResourceStats, then returns that same err. totalBatchesIndexed++ is also unsynchronized. Concurrent assignment is a data race: a failed build can be overwritten by a later nil, so group.Wait can return success after a worker failed, or a spurious error can fail startup. This now runs inside NewResourceServer and a bad initErr aborts server creation, so the race decides whether the process starts. false_positives.candidate:
Cached getForLogin drops query order

getForLogin collects delegate ids into a Set and then copies the resolved models into a HashSet before returning identityProviders.stream(). The previous uncached implementation returned the delegate stream, which is ordered (typically guiOrder / alias) for the login page. HashSet iteration order is undefined and not stable, and the order is not stored in IdentityProviderListQuery, so it cannot be reconstructed on a cache hit. Callers that do not re-sort will show identity-provider buttons in a different order on every request; only OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean sorts after the call.

Login cache can return IdPs that are no longer eligible

On a cache hit, each stored id is loaded with getById and added unconditionally. Nothing re-applies LoginFilter (enabled, not link-only, not hide-on-login, public org broker) and nothing drops a model whose organization-aware isEnabled() is now false. registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate also skips invalidation when both the wrapped original and the update still pass the login predicate and the organization id is unchanged, and organization enable/disable never touches the .idp.login keys. After an org is disabled, or after an eligibility change that the short-circuit misses, getForLogin keeps returning that broker until some unrelated login IdP is created, updated, or removed. The contract is that results are suitable for the login page; only two branches of OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean re-check isEnabled(), so every other caller keeps showing those providers.

The new clause calls idp.getConfig().get(OrganizationModel.BROKER_PUBLIC) whenever organizationId is non-null. getConfig() is not null-safe (setConfig(null) and some deserialized models leave it null), and Boolean.parseBoolean is only reached after the map dereference. getLoginPredicate() now runs on the create, update, and remove write path inside the cache provider. true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
AuthzClient.create locks in the global CryptoProvider

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) calls CryptoIntegration.init with AuthzClient's classloader. CryptoIntegration.init is process-wide and a no-op once cryptoProvider is set, so the first caller wins forever. ServiceLoader only sees META-INF/services resources of the classloader it is given. If that loader does not delegate to the server/test loader that contains DefaultCryptoProvider or FIPS1402Provider (typical with Keycloak's modular classloaders), the only hit is AuthzClientCryptoProvider. That stub then becomes the JVM-wide provider even if the server later initializes with the correct classloader. Almost every method on AuthzClientCryptoProvider throws UnsupportedOperationException, and getBouncyCastleProvider returns the platform KeyStore provider rather than BouncyCastle, so subsequent PEM, signature, and JWE operations fail or run against the wrong JCA provider.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.
Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations

false_positives.candidate:
ES384/ES512 tests use a default P-256 key

The suite generates one KeyPair via KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("EC").genKeyPair() with no ECGenParameterSpec and reuses it for ES256, ES384, and ES512. The JDK default curve is P-256, whose coordinates are 32 bytes, while ES384 and ES512 require 48-byte and 66-byte R/S values and matching curves (secp384r1, secp521r1). initSign can throw InvalidKeyException on those algorithms, or the conversion is only exercised for 32-byte integers padded out to the longer signature length. Either way the test does not prove concatenatedRSToASN1DER / asn1derToConcatenatedRS for the sizes those algorithms actually produce.

Multiple full crypto providers no longer fail closed

detectProvider now sorts by CryptoProvider.order() and silently keeps the first entry, logging the rest as ignored. DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider all return the same order (200), so a classpath that contains more than one of them no longer throws. ServiceLoader encounter order then decides which implementation is used. A FIPS deployment that accidentally also sees the non-FIPS provider can run non-FIPS crypto with no error, which is the failure mode the previous "multiple providers" check existed to prevent. FIPS needs a strictly higher order than the non-FIPS providers, and equal top orders should still be treated as a hard error.

getClientsWithPermission returns type name, not client ids

getClientsWithPermission walks every resource of type Clients and adds resource.getName() when the scope is granted. The all-clients resource is also type Clients and is named "Clients", so an all-clients grant puts the literal "Clients" into the result instead of every client id. Callers that filter the client list by this set will not include the actual clients, and a per-client grant is not combined with the type-level grant.

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close kills the shared pool and later messages are acked unprocessed

FixedQueuePool is created once on ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategies, but SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (and terminate()) always call queue_pool.shutdown(). Arroyo closes the strategy on partition revoke/rebalance and then calls create_with_partitions again on the same factory. After shutdown, Queue.put raises queue.ShutDown. submit() catches that, and the except path add_offset+complete_offset without ever running the result processor. The new strategy's commit thread then treats those offsets as done and commits them. Every message after the first rebalance is acknowledged and dropped. The offset tracker is also not reset, so a new assignment can still commit offsets for revoked partitions.

Graceful shutdown commits before workers drain

close() sets shutdown_event and joins the commit thread before queue_pool.shutdown() drains and processes remaining items. The commit loop exits after at most one commit of work that already finished. Items still queued are then processed in OrderedQueueWorker during shutdown, complete_offset runs, and nothing commits those offsets. On restart Kafka redelivers them, so uptime results are applied twice (duplicate incidents/check-ins) on every deploy or consumer restart. join() also ignores its timeout and always calls close(), so Arroyo cannot bound shutdown time.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure

Each worker queue is queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and submit() always returns after put(). The class docstring claims natural backpressure when queues fill, but the consumer thread never blocks. If result handling is slower than intake, queued WorkItems (including full Kafka messages) grow without limit until the process OOMs. Because commits cannot advance past the oldest outstanding offset, consumer lag also grows and the member can exceed max.poll.interval and be kicked from the group.

Offsets are committed from a background thread

A daemon commit_thread calls the Arroyo commit callback every second. Arroyo invokes submit/poll/close on the stream processor thread and expects commit() on that same thread; the callback updates consumer offset state and issues librdkafka commits. Calling it concurrently with poll/submit can race the consumer's in-flight commit, raise, or commit a mix of offsets the processor thread is not currently assigned. Commit should be driven from poll() (or another call on the processing thread), not a side thread.

Worker failures still advance the commit point

OrderedQueueWorker catches every Exception from result_processor, logs it, and always complete_offset in finally. get_committable_offsets then treats the message as processed and the commit loop commits past it. The strategy docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing. A transient DB or downstream error is therefore acknowledged and never retried, so uptime results are silently dropped. The same swallow exists in submit() when decode or grouping raises, which also marks the offset complete.

false_positives.candidate:
enable_advanced_features is not a paginate() argument

The new branch calls self.paginate(..., enable_advanced_features=True). Endpoint.paginate does not accept that keyword and does not forward arbitrary kwargs into the paginator constructor. The call either raises TypeError immediately or silently drops the flag, so OptimizedCursorPaginator.enable_advanced_features stays false and the branch that was supposed to change pagination never runs. The feature is also gated only by request.user.is_superuser or member.has_global_access, which is ordinary org-owner access, plus a client-controlled query param, on an unrelated spans-buffer change.

Set keys switched to sorted sets with no migration

add-buffer.lua and SpansBuffer now call ZCARD, ZUNIONSTORE, ZADD, ZSCAN, and ZPOPMIN on span-buf:s:* keys that existing consumers created with SADD/SUNIONSTORE. Redis returns WRONGTYPE if a key is still a set. During a rolling deploy, and for up to redis_ttl (default 3600s) after, insert and flush of in-flight segments fail, so spans are not buffered or cannot be flushed. There is no DEL/MIGRATE of old set keys and no WRONGTYPE handling.

ZUNIONSTORE sums scores and can double them

zunionstore is called without AGGREGATE MIN or MAX, so Redis's default SUM applies. When the same payload is already in both the destination segment key and the key being merged (retry, or span_key equal to set_key), the end_timestamp_precise score is added to itself. Eviction uses ZPOPMIN on those scores, so the wrong spans are dropped and ordering no longer matches end timestamps. The call should aggregate with MIN or MAX so a member keeps a single timestamp.

Redirect walk cap cut from 10000 to 1000

The parent-redirect loop now stops at 1000 hops and the comment that this cap can fail to join deep segment trees was removed. On exit, the script still HSETs span_id to whatever set_span_id it stopped on and merges only that key. Traces whose redirect chain is deeper than 1000 are stored as split segments and later flushed with the wrong segment id, which the previous 10000 cap was explicitly there to avoid.

Hardcoded eviction drops spans with no metric or config

After merge, if the zset has more than 1000 members the script ZPOPMINs span_count-1000 members (lowest end_timestamp_precise) and returns success. The Python max_segment_spans limit (1001) and the flush-time segment_span_count_exceeded metric/error log were removed, and the cap is not passed into the script. The consumer will commit offsets for spans that were just deleted, with no signal that data was dropped, and the cap cannot be tuned via SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans. Eviction also runs on a span_count that stays 0-initialized unless a union happened, falling back to ZCARD only in that case; a union result that does not reflect members added only on the other key can under-count and leave the segment over the cap, or the next insert will delete the oldest payload including a root span while the has-root flag remains set.

Nothing in this change calls the invalidator when the allowlist option changes, so a stable key would still be stale for up to 60s.

Check returns Allowed=false as soon as a denial-cache entry exists for (namespace, subject, action, name, parent), before consulting either the permission cache or the database. Entries are written for every deny and kept for shortCacheTTL (30s), and nothing deletes them when a role, team, or creator grant later adds that scope. A user who was denied on a dashboard or folder they then create or are granted will keep getting denied until TTL, which is the failure this PR is meant to fix. Only the in-proc client is switched to NoopCache. newRemoteRBACClient still wraps the gRPC client in a local cache with a 30s expiry. false_positives.candidate:
Installer identity check is skipped when no Integration row exists

GitHubInstallation only compares pipeline state github_authenticated_user to metadata sender when an Integration for installation_id already exists, has no OrganizationIntegration, and is ACTIVE. If Integration.DoesNotExist, dispatch returns pipeline.next_step() immediately and never consults the OAuth login. Installation IDs are predictable integers and are supplied by the client (query string or earlier bind_state). An attacker who starts the install pipeline in their own Sentry org and supplies a victim installation_id before the installation webhook creates the Integration will pass this gate, and build_integration will attach that GitHub App installation to the attacker org with no check that the OAuth user is the installer. That is the mismatch this change claims to reject, and it is unenforced on the normal first-install path.

Token exchange omits redirect_uri required by the authorize request

OAuthLoginView sends redirect_uri on the GitHub authorize redirect, but the subsequent POST to the access-token URL only sends code, client_id, and client_secret. GitHub requires the same redirect_uri on the token exchange when it was included in the authorization request. The exchange will be rejected, access_token will be missing, and every install will fall through to the generic invalid-installation error. Tests stub the token endpoint and never assert the POST body, so they do not catch this.

OAuth authorize URL is built by string concatenation without encoding

The authorize redirect interpolates client_id, state, and redirect_uri into the query string with no urlencode. redirect_uri comes from absolute_uri() and is not escaped, so any reserved character (&, #, ?) splits or drops parameters. state and client_id are likewise unescaped. A crafted or future redirect_uri can change which parameters GitHub sees (for example dropping or replacing state), which weakens the CSRF check this view just added. Use urllib.parse.urlencode for the query.

The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.

The new strategy's commit thread then treats those offsets as done and commits them. Every message after the first rebalance is acknowledged and dropped. On restart Kafka redelivers them, so uptime results are applied twice (duplicate incidents/check-ins) on every deploy or consumer restart. join() also ignores its timeout and always calls close(), so Arroyo cannot bound shutdown time.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure

Each worker queue is queue.Queue() with no maxsize, and submit() always returns after put(). The class docstring claims natural backpressure when queues fill, but the consumer thread never blocks. If result handling is slower than intake, queued WorkItems (including full Kafka messages) grow without limit until the process OOMs. Because commits cannot advance past the oldest outstanding offset, consumer lag also grows and the member can exceed max.poll.interval and be kicked from the group.

Offsets are committed from a background thread

A daemon commit_thread calls the Arroyo commit callback every second. Arroyo invokes submit/poll/close on the stream processor thread and expects commit() on that same thread; the callback updates consumer offset state and issues librdkafka commits. Calling it concurrently with poll/submit can race the consumer's in-flight commit, raise, or commit a mix of offsets the processor thread is not currently assigned. Commit should be driven from poll() (or another call on the processing thread), not a side thread.

Worker failures still advance the commit point

OrderedQueueWorker catches every Exception from result_processor, logs it, and always complete_offset in finally. get_committable_offsets then treats the message as processed and the commit loop commits past it. The strategy docstring says offsets are committed only after successful processing. A transient DB or downstream error is therefore acknowledged and never retried, so uptime results are silently dropped. The same swallow exists in submit() when decode or grouping raises, which also marks the offset complete.
